newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Work under way to build nuclear plants in N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: Work under way to build nuclear plants in N.Korea.

text.p: South Korean workers on Wednesday prepared to build two nuclear reactors in North Korea, but Seoul officials said it would probably take a decade before these would ease Pyongyang's crippling power shortage.

Officials at the Korean Peninsula Energy Development Organisation (KEDO), an international consortium in charge of building the plants, said the impoverished North would have to overhaul its ageing power system to handle such modern plants.

They said South Korean vessels carrying 9,000 tonnes of bulldozers, trucks and heavy equipment arrived at the North Korean port of Yanghwa on Wednesday to clear land at the site of the project in the coastal town of Sinpo.
KEDO opened a liaison office this week to oversee the project, and 80 South Korean workers are helping in preparations to link the nuclear site to the port so that equipment can be delivered.
"North Korea's electricity is currently so weak and unstable we can't run a copy machine or use our PCs on it," said a senior KEDO official in Seoul who declined to be identified.
"For the plant construction, we are taking our own generators."

The preliminary work should have started more than a year ago under a landmark U.S.-North Korea deal in 1994, under which Pyongyang agreed to abandon its suspected nuclear weapons programme in return for the $4.5 billion project.

But the signing of a major contract for the supply of the reactors between KEDO and North Korea was delayed for about eight months. Heightened tensions on the peninsula after the grounding last September of a northern submarine on a southern beach also put KEDO's work on hold for several months.
KEDO is led by the United States, South Korea and Japan, but the South is largely responsible for the construction of the plants as it is bearing the lion's share of the total cost.

Experts fear the North's power transmission network is too small and old for the 1,000-megawatt light-water reactors. They say the communist state is aware of the problem but might not have the funds to upgrade infrastructure.
Also, the grid system is not computerised, which could hinder distribution and even possibly trip the reactors, they added.

Unless the North increases its generating capacity, now estimated at between 7,400-11,000 megawatts, heavy reliance on nuclear sources could also disrupt the power supply if the reactors are shut down for repair or loading of fuel rods, they said.

"As a rule of thumb, if any one unit exceeds 10 percent of the system's capacity, it makes the system unstable," said Cho Sung-bong, who heads the electricity policy division at South Korea's trade, industry and energy ministry's think-tank.

Seoul's Unification Ministry said less then 30 percent of the North's factories were operating at present because of an acute energy shortage. Many thermo-electric generators have also been shut down.
With the North Korean economy in ruins, one solution for the funding problem is through economic cooperation between the two Koreas, Cho said.
"The South has problems finding sites for new reactors because no one wants them in their neighbourhood, and the North doesn't have money for upgrading its system," he said.
"For reunification, we will inevitably have to pay a cost," Cho added. "Connecting the North and South Korean power systems and helping the North can be an investment for the future."
KEDO officials said such cooperation would require an end to the fierce Cold War confrontation that has persisted between the two Koreas since the 1950-53 Korean War.
"It is not realistic to talk about such a solution at this stage," one official said.
